blocks.text_en: 1. Introduction
blocks.html: 1. Introduction

blocks.text_en:
The TOGAF ® Standard is a framework for Enterprise Architecture. It may be
used freely by any organization wishing to develop an Enterprise
Architecture for use within that organization; see Section 1.3.1, “Conditions of Use” .
blocks.html: The TOGAF® Standard is a framework for Enterprise Architecture. It may be used freely by any organization wishing to develop an Enterprise Architecture for use within that organization; see Section 1.3.1, “Conditions of Use”.

blocks.text_en:
The TOGAF Standard is developed and maintained by members of The Open
Group, working within the Architecture Forum (refer to www.opengroup.org/architecture-forum ).
The original development of TOGAF Version 1 in 1995 was based on the
Technical Architecture Framework for Information Management (TAFIM),

developed by the US Department of Defense (DoD). The DoD gave The Open
Group explicit permission and encouragement to create Version 1 of the
TOGAF Standard by building on the TAFIM, which itself was the result of
many years of development effort and many millions of dollars of US
Government investment.

The DoD gave The Open Group explicit permission and encouragement to create Version 1 of the TOGAF Standard by building on the TAFIM, which itself was the result of many years of development effort and many millions of dollars of US Government investment.

blocks.text_en:
Starting from this sound foundation, the members of The Open Group
Architecture Forum have developed successive versions of the TOGAF
Standard and published each one on The Open Group public website.
blocks.html: Starting from this sound foundation, the members of The Open Group Architecture Forum have developed successive versions of the TOGAF Standard and published each one on The Open Group public website.

blocks.text_en:
This version builds on previous versions of the TOGAF Standard and
updates the material available to architecture practitioners to assist
them in building a sustainable Enterprise Architecture. Work on White
Papers and Guides describing how to integrate and use this standard with
other frameworks and architectural styles has highlighted the universal
framework parts of the standard, as well as industry, architecture
style, and purpose-specific tools, techniques, and guidance. This work
is embodied in the TOGAF Library. [ 1 ]

Work on White Papers and Guides describing how to integrate and use this standard with other frameworks and architectural styles has highlighted the universal framework parts of the standard, as well as industry, architecture style, and purpose-specific tools, techniques, and guidance. This work is embodied in the TOGAF Library.[1]

expected that organizations will customize it during adoption, and
deliberately choose some elements, customize some, exclude some, and
create others. For example, an organization may wish to adopt the TOGAF metamodel, but elect not to use any of the guidance on how to develop an in-house Technology Architecture because they are heavy consumers of cloud services.

blocks.text_en: 1.1. Executive Overview

blocks.text_en:
This section provides an executive overview of Enterprise Architecture,
the basic concepts of what it is (not just another name for IT
Architecture), and why it is needed. It provides a summary of the
benefits of establishing an Enterprise Architecture and adopting the TOGAF approach to achieve that.

blocks.text_en: What is an Enterprise?
blocks.html: What is an Enterprise?

blocks.text_en: The TOGAF Standard considers an “enterprise” to be any collection of organizations that have common goals. For example, an enterprise could be:
blocks.html: The TOGAF Standard considers an “enterprise” to be any collection of organizations that have common goals. For example, an enterprise could be:

blocks.text_en:
A whole corporation or a division of a corporation A government agency or a single government department A chain of geographically distant organizations linked together by
common ownership Groups of countries, governments, or governmental organizations (such
as militaries) working together to create common or shareable
deliverables or infrastructures Partnerships and alliances of businesses working together, such as a
consortium or supply chain
blocks.html:
• A whole corporation or a division of a corporation

  • A government agency or a single government department

  • A chain of geographically distant organizations linked together by common ownership

  • Groups of countries, governments, or governmental organizations (such as militaries) working together to create common or shareable deliverables or infrastructures

  • Partnerships and alliances of businesses working together, such as a consortium or supply chain

blocks.text_en:
The term “Enterprise” in the context of “Enterprise Architecture” can be
applied to either an entire enterprise, encompassing all of its business
activities and capabilities, information, and technology that make up
the entire infrastructure and governance of the enterprise, or to one or
more specific areas of interest within the enterprise. An enterprise may
include partners, suppliers, and customers as well as internal business
units. In all cases, the architecture crosses multiple systems, and
multiple functional groups within the enterprise.

An enterprise may include partners, suppliers, and customers as well as internal business units. In all cases, the architecture crosses multiple systems, and multiple functional groups within the enterprise.

blocks.text_en:
The enterprise operating model concept is useful to determine the nature
and scope of the Enterprise Architecture within an organization. Many
organizations may comprise multiple enterprises, and may develop and
maintain a number of independent Enterprise Architectures to address
each one. These enterprises often have much in common with each other
including processes, functions, and their information systems, and there
is often great potential for wider gain in the use of a common
architecture framework. For example, a common framework can provide a
basis for the development of common building blocks and solutions, and a
shareable Architecture Repository for the integration and re-use of
business models, designs, information, and data.

blocks.text_en: Why is an Enterprise Architecture Needed?
blocks.html: Why is an Enterprise Architecture Needed?

blocks.text_en:
The purpose of Enterprise Architecture is to optimize across the
enterprise the often fragmented legacy of processes (both manual and
automated) into an integrated environment that is responsive to change
and supportive of the delivery of the business strategy.
blocks.html: The purpose of Enterprise Architecture is to optimize across the enterprise the often fragmented legacy of processes (both manual and automated) into an integrated environment that is responsive to change and supportive of the delivery of the business strategy.

blocks.text_en:
The effective management and exploitation of information and Digital
Transformation are key factors to business success, and indispensable
means to achieving competitive advantage. An Enterprise Architecture
addresses this need, by providing a strategic context for the evolution
and reach of digital capability in response to the constantly changing
needs of the business environment.
blocks.html: The effective management and exploitation of information and Digital Transformation are key factors to business success, and indispensable means to achieving competitive advantage. An Enterprise Architecture addresses this need, by providing a strategic context for the evolution and reach of digital capability in response to the constantly changing needs of the business environment.

blocks.text_en:

right balance between business transformation and continuous operational
efficiency. It allows individual business units to innovate safely in
their pursuit of evolving business goals and competitive advantage. At
the same time, the Enterprise Architecture enables the needs of the
organization to be met with an integrated strategy which permits the
closest possible synergies across the enterprise and beyond.

blocks.text_en: What is an Architecture Framework
blocks.html: What is an Architecture Framework

blocks.text_en:
An architecture framework is a foundational structure, or set of
structures, which can be used for developing a broad range of different architectures. It should include a method for describing both a baseline and target state of the enterprise, in terms of a set of building blocks for showing how the building blocks fit together and planning the evolution from baseline to target states.

blocks.text_en:
A framework is typically tailored to meet the specific needs of the
organization. Tailoring of the framework should establish a set of tools and a common vocabulary.

blocks.text_en: Why Use the TOGAF Standard as a Framework for Enterprise Architecture?
blocks.html: Why Use the TOGAF Standard as a Framework for Enterprise Architecture?

blocks.text_en: The TOGAF Standard has been developed through the collaborative efforts of the whole community. Using the TOGAF Standard results in Enterprise Architecture that is consistent, reflects the needs of stakeholders, employs best practice, and gives due consideration both to current requirements and the perceived future needs of the business.

Using the TOGAF Standard results in Enterprise Architecture that is consistent, reflects the needs of stakeholders, employs best practice, and gives due consideration both to current requirements and the perceived future needs of the business.

The TOGAF Standard provides a best practice framework for adding value, and enables the organization to build workable and economic solutions which address their business issues and needs.

operate in an efficient and effective way using a proven and recognized set of best practices, across the enterprise and in different sectors to address specific business and technology trends.

blocks.text_en: When Should Enterprise Architecture be Done?
blocks.html: When Should Enterprise Architecture be Done?

blocks.text_en:
To get the greatest benefit from Enterprise Architecture it should be done early and throughout the change process to help decision-makers understand the implications of their decisions. Without this
understanding, costly mistakes can be made and Enterprise Architecture is not serving its fullest potential. Enterprise Architecture done after decisions are made is merely documentation of those decisions or at best enforcement of those decisions. No insight is gained as to the effect of those decisions which could be far-reaching and perhaps detrimental.

establishing an architecture framework, developing architecture content,

use:
blocks.html: The Architecture Content Framework uses the following three categories to describe the type of architectural work product within the context of use:

blocks.text_en:
A deliverable is a work product that is contractually specified and
in turn formally reviewed, approved, and signed off by the stakeholders Deliverables represent the output of projects and those deliverables
that are in documentation form will typically be archived at completion
of a project, or transitioned into an Architecture Repository as a
reference model, standard, or snapshot of the Architecture Landscape at
a point in time. An artifact is an architectural work product that describes an
aspect of the architecture Artifacts are generally classified as catalogs (lists of things),
matrices (showing relationships between things), and diagrams (pictures
of things). Examples include a requirements catalog, application
interaction matrix, and a value chain diagram. An architectural
deliverable may contain one or more artifacts and artifacts will form
the content of the Architecture Repository. An artifact may or may not
be considered a deliverable based on the contractual specification. A building block represents a potentially re-usable component that
can be combined with other building blocks to deliver architectures and
solutions Building blocks can be defined at various levels of detail, depending on
what stage of architecture development has been reached. For instance,
at an early stage, a building block can simply consist of a name or an
outline description. Later on, a building block may be decomposed into
multiple supporting building blocks and may be accompanied by a full
specification. Building blocks can relate to “architectures” or
“solutions”. Architecture Building Blocks (ABBs) typically describe required
capability and shape the specification of Solution Building Blocks
(SBBs); for example, a customer services capability may be required
within an enterprise, supported by many SBBs, such as processes, data,
and application software Solution Building Blocks (SBBs) represent actual implementation choices to realize a required capability; for example, a network is an ABB that can be realized by different implementation choices (SBBs), such as a satellite network in two major configurations: a hive of myriad microsatellites or a small set of large satellites
blocks.html:
• A deliverable is a work product that is contractually specified and in turn formally reviewed, approved, and signed off by the stakeholders

    Deliverables represent the output of projects and those deliverables that are in documentation form will typically be archived at completion of a project, or transitioned into an Architecture Repository as a reference model, standard, or snapshot of the Architecture Landscape at a point in time.

  • An artifact is an architectural work product that describes an aspect of the architecture

    Artifacts are generally classified as catalogs (lists of things), matrices (showing relationships between things), and diagrams (pictures of things). Examples include a requirements catalog, application interaction matrix, and a value chain diagram. An architectural deliverable may contain one or more artifacts and artifacts will form the content of the Architecture Repository.   • A building block represents a potentially re-usable component that can be combined with other building blocks to deliver architectures and solutions

For instance, at an early stage, a building block can simply consist of a name or an outline description.     • Architecture Building Blocks (ABBs) typically describe required capability and shape the specification of Solution Building Blocks (SBBs); for example, a customer services capability may be required within an enterprise, supported by many SBBs, such as processes, data, and application software

    • Solution Building Blocks (SBBs) represent actual implementation choices to realize a required capability; for example, a network is an ABB that can be realized by different implementation choices (SBBs), such as a satellite network in two major configurations: a hive of myriad microsatellites or a small set of large satellites

blocks.text_en: 3.7. Architecture Abstraction
blocks.html: 3.7. Architecture Abstraction

blocks.text_en: A process or technique for creating simplified views of a system-of-interest, for the purpose of discussion, communication, and decision-making about some aspect of the system, pertinent to its stakeholders.
blocks.html: A process or technique for creating simplified views of a system-of-interest, for the purpose of discussion, communication, and decision-making about some aspect of the system, pertinent to its stakeholders.

blocks.text_en:
Abstraction levels are layered in nature, moving from high-level models
to more detailed models.
blocks.html: Abstraction levels are layered in nature, moving from high-level models to more detailed models.

blocks.text_en:
Architecture effort can be divided into four distinct abstraction levels
that cross the Business, Data, Application, and Technology domains to
answer fundamental questions about an architecture:
blocks.html: Architecture effort can be divided into four distinct abstraction levels that cross the Business, Data, Application, and Technology domains to answer fundamental questions about an architecture:

blocks.text_en:
Why — why is the architecture needed? What — what functionality and other requirements need to be met by the
architecture? How — how do we structure the functionality? With what — with what assets shall we implement this structure?
blocks.html:
• Why — why is the architecture needed?

  • What — what functionality and other requirements need to be met by the architecture?

  • How — how do we structure the functionality?

  • With what — with what assets shall we implement this structure?

blocks.text_en:
Note that why, what, and how have no connection to their use in the
Zachman ® Enterprise Architecture Framework.
blocks.html: Note that why, what, and how have no connection to their use in the Zachman® Enterprise Architecture Framework.

blocks.text_en: 3.7.1. Contextual Abstraction Level
blocks.html: 3.7.1. Contextual Abstraction Level

blocks.text_en:
This abstraction level is focused on understanding the environment in
which an enterprise operates and the context in which architecture work
is planned and executed. It answers why an enterprise undertakes
architecture work, what is the scope of work, and the motivation in
terms of goals, drivers, and objectives.
blocks.html: This abstraction level is focused on understanding the environment in which an enterprise operates and the context in which architecture work is planned and executed. It answers why an enterprise undertakes architecture work, what is the scope of work, and the motivation in terms of goals, drivers, and objectives.

blocks.text_en: 3.7.2. Conceptual Abstraction Level
blocks.html: 3.7.2. Conceptual Abstraction Level

blocks.text_en:
This abstraction level is centered on decomposing the requirements to
understand the problem, and what is needed to address the problem,
without unduly focusing on how the architecture will be realized. It
answers what is necessary to realize the requirements and is usually
modeled using service models (business service, application service,
technology service) that represent desired behavior.
blocks.html: This abstraction level is centered on decomposing the requirements to understand the problem, and what is needed to address the problem, without unduly focusing on how the architecture will be realized. It answers what is necessary to realize the requirements and is usually modeled using service models (business service, application service, technology service) that represent desired behavior.

blocks.text_en:
Note this abstraction level can also be referred to as either service
abstraction or behavior abstraction.
blocks.html: Note this abstraction level can also be referred to as either service abstraction or behavior abstraction.

blocks.text_en: 3.7.3. Logical Abstraction Level
blocks.html: 3.7.3. Logical Abstraction Level

blocks.text_en:
This abstraction level is focused on identifying the kinds of business,
data, application, and technology components needed to achieve the
services identified in the conceptual level. It is about identifying how an architecture can be organized and structured, in an
implementation-independent fashion. There will potentially be several ways to group services into logical components, based on principles and
other grouping criteria, providing different logical solution alternatives.
blocks.html: This abstraction level is focused on identifying the kinds of business, data, application, and technology components needed to achieve the services identified in the conceptual level. It is about identifying how an architecture can be organized and structured, in an implementation-independent fashion. There will potentially be several ways to group services into logical components, based on principles and other grouping criteria, providing different logical solution alternatives.

blocks.text_en: 3.7.4. Physical Abstraction Level
blocks.html: 3.7.4. Physical Abstraction Level

blocks.text_en:
This abstraction level manages the allocation and implementation of
physical components to meet the identified logical components. It is about determining with what physical components the logical-level components can be realized. There will potentially be many ways to use
physical components to realize logical components, based on principles and other grouping criteria, providing different physical solution
alternatives.
blocks.html: This abstraction level manages the allocation and implementation of physical components to meet the identified logical components. It is about determining with what physical components the logical-level components can be realized. There will potentially be many ways to use physical components to realize logical components, based on principles and other grouping criteria, providing different physical solution alternatives.

blocks.text_en: 3.8. Architecture Principles
blocks.html: 3.8. Architecture Principles

blocks.text_en:
Principles are general rules and guidelines, intended to be enduring and
seldom amended, that inform and support the way in which an organization
sets about fulfilling its mission.
blocks.html: Principles are general rules and guidelines, intended to be enduring and seldom amended, that inform and support the way in which an organization sets about fulfilling its mission.

blocks.text_en:
Depending on the organization, principles may be established within
different domains and at different levels. Two key domains inform the
development and utilization of architecture:
blocks.html: Depending on the organization, principles may be established within different domains and at different levels. Two key domains inform the development and utilization of architecture:

blocks.text_en:
Enterprise Principles provide a basis for decision-making throughout
an enterprise, and inform how the organization sets about fulfilling its
mission Enterprise Principles define the underlying general rules and
guidelines for the use and deployment of all resources and assets across the enterprise. They reflect a level of consensus among the various elements of the enterprise . Such principles are commonly found as a means of harmonizing
decision-making across an organization. In particular, they are a key
element in a successful Architecture Governance strategy (see TOGAF Standard — EA Capability and Governance ). Within the broad domain of Enterprise Principles, it is common to have
subsidiary principles within a business or organizational unit; for
example, principles specific to IT, HR, domestic operations, or overseas
operations. These principles provide a basis for decision-making within
the subsidiary domain and will inform architecture development within
the domain. Care must be taken to ensure that the principles used to
inform architecture development align to the organizational context of
the Architecture Capability. Architecture Principles are a set of principles that relate to
architecture work They reflect a level of consensus across the enterprise and embody the
spirit and thinking of existing Enterprise Principles. Architecture
Principles govern the architecture process, affecting the development,
maintenance, and use of the Enterprise Architecture.
blocks.html:
• Enterprise Principles provide a basis for decision-making throughout an enterprise, and inform how the organization sets about fulfilling its mission

    Enterprise Principles define the underlying general rules and guidelines for the use and deployment of all resources and assets across the enterprise. They reflect a level of consensus among the various elements of the enterprise .

    Such principles are commonly found as a means of harmonizing decision-making across an organization. In particular, they are a key element in a successful Architecture Governance strategy (see TOGAF Standard — EA Capability and Governance).

    Within the broad domain of Enterprise Principles, it is common to have subsidiary principles within a business or organizational unit; for example, principles specific to IT, HR, domestic operations, or overseas operations. These principles provide a basis for decision-making within the subsidiary domain and will inform architecture development within the domain. Care must be taken to ensure that the principles used to inform architecture development align to the organizational context of the Architecture Capability.

  • Architecture Principles are a set of principles that relate to architecture work

    They reflect a level of consensus across the enterprise and embody the spirit and thinking of existing Enterprise Principles. Architecture Principles govern the architecture process, affecting the development, maintenance, and use of the Enterprise Architecture.

blocks.text_en:
Within an enterprise the hierarchy of principles starts with the
Enterprise Principles. The subsidiary segment principles must exist
within the bounds of these Enterprise Principles which are overarching.
Consequently, at each hierarchical level the set of principles will be
informed by and elaborate on the principles inherited from the level
above and cannot overstep their boundaries.
blocks.html: Within an enterprise the hierarchy of principles starts with the Enterprise Principles. The subsidiary segment principles must exist within the bounds of these Enterprise Principles which are overarching. Consequently, at each hierarchical level the set of principles will be informed by and elaborate on the principles inherited from the level above and cannot overstep their boundaries.

blocks.text_en: Architecture Principles may restate other enterprise guidance in terms and form that effectively guide architecture development.
blocks.html: Architecture Principles may restate other enterprise guidance in terms and form that effectively guide architecture development.

blocks.text_en: The architecture should be clearly relatable to Principles for the manner in which it realizes objectives responding to drivers.
blocks.html: The architecture should be clearly relatable to Principles for the manner in which it realizes objectives responding to drivers.

blocks.text_en: Architecture Principles are further explained in the TOGAF Standard — ADM Techniques .
blocks.html: Architecture Principles are further explained in the TOGAF Standard — ADM Techniques.

blocks.text_en: 3.9. Interoperability
blocks.html: 3.9. Interoperability

blocks.text_en:
A definition of interoperability is “the ability to share information and services”. Defining the degree to which the information and services
are or are not to be shared is a very useful architectural requirement,
especially in a complex organization and/or extended enterprise.
blocks.html: A definition of interoperability is “the ability to share information and services”. Defining the degree to which the information and services are or are not to be shared is a very useful architectural requirement, especially in a complex organization and/or extended enterprise.

blocks.text_en:
The determination of interoperability is present throughout the
Architecture Development Method (ADM) as follows:
blocks.html: The determination of interoperability is present throughout the Architecture Development Method (ADM) as follows:

blocks.text_en:
In the Architecture Vision (Phase A), the nature and security
considerations of the information and service exchanges are first
revealed within the business scenarios In the Business Architecture (Phase B), the information and service exchanges are further defined in business terms In the Data Architecture (Phase C), the content of the information exchanges is detailed using the corporate data and/or information
exchange model In the Application Architecture (Phase C), the way that the various
applications are to share the information and services is specified In the Technology Architecture (Phase D), the appropriate technical
mechanisms to permit the information and service exchanges are specified In Opportunities & Solutions (Phase E), the actual solutions (e.g.,
Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) packages) are selected In Migration Planning (Phase F), the interoperability is logically
implemented
blocks.html:
• In the Architecture Vision (Phase A), the nature and security considerations of the information and service exchanges are first revealed within the business scenarios

  • In the Business Architecture (Phase B), the information and service exchanges are further defined in business terms

  • In the Data Architecture (Phase C), the content of the information exchanges is detailed using the corporate data and/or information exchange model

  • In the Application Architecture (Phase C), the way that the various applications are to share the information and services is specified

  • In the Technology Architecture (Phase D), the appropriate technical mechanisms to permit the information and service exchanges are specified

  • In Opportunities & Solutions (Phase E), the actual solutions (e.g., Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) packages) are selected

  • In Migration Planning (Phase F), the interoperability is logically implemented

blocks.text_en:
There are many ways to define interoperability and the aim is to define
one that is consistently applied within the enterprise and extended
enterprise. It is best that both the enterprise and the extended
enterprise use the same definitions.
blocks.html: There are many ways to define interoperability and the aim is to define one that is consistently applied within the enterprise and extended enterprise. It is best that both the enterprise and the extended enterprise use the same definitions.

blocks.text_en:
Many organizations find it useful to categorize interoperability as
follows:
blocks.html: Many organizations find it useful to categorize interoperability as follows:

blocks.text_en:
Operational or Business Interoperability defines how different parts
of the enterprise work together at the business level Information Interoperability defines how information is to be shared Technical Interoperability defines how technical resources are to be
shared or at least connect to one another
blocks.html:
• Operational or Business Interoperability defines how different parts of the enterprise work together at the business level

  • Information Interoperability defines how information is to be shared

  • Technical Interoperability defines how technical resources are to be shared or at least connect to one another
From an IT perspective, it is also useful to consider interoperability in a similar vein to Enterprise Application Integration (EAI); specifically:

blocks.text_en:
Presentation Integration/Interoperability is where a common
look-and-feel approach through a common portal-like solution guides the
user to the underlying functionality of the set of systems Information Integration/Interoperability is where the corporate
information is seamlessly shared between the various corporate
applications to achieve, for example, a common set of client information Normally this is based upon a commonly accepted corporate ontology and
shared services for the structure, quality, access, and security/privacy
for the information. Application Integration/Interoperability is where the corporate
functionality is integrated and shareable so that the applications are
not duplicated (e.g., one change of address service/component; not one
for every application) and are seamlessly linked together through
functionality such as workflow This impacts the business and infrastructure applications and is very
closely linked to corporate business process unification/interoperability. Technical Integration/Interoperability includes common methods and shared services for the communication, storage, processing, and access to data primarily in the application platform and communications
infrastructure domains
blocks.html:
• Presentation Integration/Interoperability is where a common look-and-feel approach through a common portal-like solution guides the user to the underlying functionality of the set of systems

  • Information Integration/Interoperability is where the corporate information is seamlessly shared between the various corporate applications to achieve, for example, a common set of client information

    Normally this is based upon a commonly accepted corporate ontology and shared services for the structure, quality, access, and security/privacy for the information.

  • Application Integration/Interoperability is where the corporate functionality is integrated and shareable so that the applications are not duplicated (e.g., one change of address service/component; not one for every application) and are seamlessly linked together through functionality such as workflow

    This impacts the business and infrastructure applications and is very closely linked to corporate business process unification/interoperability.

  • Technical Integration/Interoperability includes common methods and shared services for the communication, storage, processing, and access to data primarily in the application platform and communications infrastructure domains

blocks.text_en: Interoperability and Interoperability Requirements are addressed in detail in the TOGAF Standard — ADM Techniques .
blocks.html: Interoperability and Interoperability Requirements are addressed in detail in the TOGAF Standard — ADM Techniques.

blocks.text_en: 3.10. Enterprise Continuum
blocks.html: 3.10. Enterprise Continuum

blocks.text_en:
The TOGAF Standard includes the concept of the Enterprise Continuum, which sets the broader context for an architect and explains how generic
solutions can be leveraged and specialized in order to support the requirements of an individual organization.
blocks.html: The TOGAF Standard includes the concept of the Enterprise Continuum, which sets the broader context for an architect and explains how generic solutions can be leveraged and specialized in order to support the requirements of an individual organization.

blocks.text_en:
The Enterprise Continuum is a categorization for assets held in the
Enterprise Repositories that provides methods for classifying assets,
including architecture and solution artifacts as they evolve from
generic Foundation Architectures to Organization-Specific Architectures.
The Enterprise Continuum comprises two complementary concepts: the Architecture Continuum and the Solutions Continuum.
blocks.html: The Enterprise Continuum is a categorization for assets held in the Enterprise Repositories that provides methods for classifying assets, including architecture and solution artifacts as they evolve from generic Foundation Architectures to Organization-Specific Architectures. The Enterprise Continuum comprises two complementary concepts: the Architecture Continuum and the Solutions Continuum.

blocks.text_en: The Enterprise Continuum is described in detail in the TOGAF Standard — Architecture Content .
blocks.html: The Enterprise Continuum is described in detail in the TOGAF Standard — Architecture Content.

blocks.text_en:
An overview of the structure and context for the Enterprise Continuum is
shown in Figure 3-4 .
blocks.html: An overview of the structure and context for the Enterprise Continuum is shown in Figure 3-4.

blocks.text_en: Figure 3-4: Enterprise Continuum
3.10.1. Architecture Repository
blocks.html: 3.10.1. Architecture Repository

blocks.text_en:
Supporting the Enterprise Continuum is the concept of an Architecture Repository which can be used to store different classes of architectural
output at different levels of abstraction, created by the ADM. In this way, the TOGAF Standard facilitates understanding and co-operation
between stakeholders and practitioners at different levels.
blocks.html: Supporting the Enterprise Continuum is the concept of an Architecture Repository which can be used to store different classes of architectural output at different levels of abstraction, created by the ADM. In this way, the TOGAF Standard facilitates understanding and co-operation between stakeholders and practitioners at different levels.

blocks.text_en:
By means of the Enterprise Continuum and Architecture Repository,
architects are encouraged to leverage all other relevant architectural
resources and assets in developing an Organization-Specific
Architecture. In this context, the TOGAF ADM can be regarded as
describing a process lifecycle that operates at multiple levels within the organization, operating within a holistic governance framework and
producing aligned outputs that reside in an Architecture Repository. The
Enterprise Continuum provides a valuable context for understanding
architectural models: it shows building blocks and their relationships
to each other, and the constraints and requirements on a cycle of architecture development.
blocks.html: By means of the Enterprise Continuum and Architecture Repository, architects are encouraged to leverage all other relevant architectural resources and assets in developing an Organization-Specific Architecture. In this context, the TOGAF ADM can be regarded as describing a process lifecycle that operates at multiple levels within the organization, operating within a holistic governance framework and producing aligned outputs that reside in an Architecture Repository. The Enterprise Continuum provides a valuable context for understanding architectural models: it shows building blocks and their relationships to each other, and the constraints and requirements on a cycle of architecture development.

blocks.text_en: The structure of the TOGAF Architecture Repository is shown in Figure 3-5 .
blocks.html: The structure of the TOGAF Architecture Repository is shown in Figure 3-5.

blocks.text_en: Figure 3-5: TOGAF Architecture Repository Structure
The major components within an Architecture Repository are as follows:
blocks.html: The major components within an Architecture Repository are as follows:

blocks.text_en:
The Architecture Metamodel describes the organizationally tailored
application of an architecture framework, including a metamodel for architecture content The Architecture Capability defines the parameters, structures, and
processes that support governance of the Architecture Repository The Architecture Landscape is the architectural representation of
assets deployed within the operating enterprise at a particular point in
time — the landscape is likely to exist at multiple levels of
abstraction to suit different architecture objectives The Standards Library captures the standards with which new
architectures must comply, which may include industry standards,
selected products and services from suppliers, or shared services
already deployed within the organization The Reference Library provides guidelines, templates, patterns, and
other forms of reference material that can be leveraged in order to
accelerate the creation of new architectures for the enterprise The Governance Repository provides a record of governance activity
across the enterprise The Architecture Requirements Repository provides a view of all
authorized architecture requirements which have been agreed with the
Architecture Board The Solutions Landscape presents an architectural representation of
the SBBs supporting the Architecture Landscape which have been planned
or deployed by the enterprise
blocks.html:
• The Architecture Metamodel describes the organizationally tailored application of an architecture framework, including a metamodel for architecture content

  • The Architecture Capability defines the parameters, structures, and processes that support governance of the Architecture Repository

  • The Architecture Landscape is the architectural representation of assets deployed within the operating enterprise at a particular point in time — the landscape is likely to exist at multiple levels of abstraction to suit different architecture objectives

  • The Standards Library captures the standards with which new architectures must comply, which may include industry standards, selected products and services from suppliers, or shared services already deployed within the organization

  • The Reference Library provides guidelines, templates, patterns, and other forms of reference material that can be leveraged in order to accelerate the creation of new architectures for the enterprise

  • The Governance Repository provides a record of governance activity across the enterprise

  • The Architecture Requirements Repository provides a view of all authorized architecture requirements which have been agreed with the Architecture Board

  • The Solutions Landscape presents an architectural representation of the SBBs supporting the Architecture Landscape which have been planned or deployed by the enterprise

blocks.text_en: 3.18. Risk Management
blocks.html: 3.18. Risk Management

blocks.text_en: There will always be risk with any architecture/business transformation effort. It is important to identify, classify, and mitigate these risks before starting so that they can be tracked throughout the transformation effort.

blocks.text_en:
Mitigation is an ongoing effort and often the risk triggers may be
outside the scope of the transformation planners (e.g., merger,
acquisition) so planners must monitor the transformation context
constantly.

the risks and mitigate certain ones, but it is within the governance
framework that risks have to be first accepted and then managed.

blocks.html: 4.42. EA Landscape

blocks.text_en: See Section 4.15, “Architecture Landscape” .
blocks.html: See Section 4.15, “Architecture Landscape”.

blocks.text_en: 4.43. Enterprise
blocks.html: 4.43. Enterprise

blocks.text_en:
The highest level (typically) of description of an organization and
typically covers all missions and functions. An enterprise will often
span multiple organizations.
blocks.html: The highest level (typically) of description of an organization and typically covers all missions and functions. An enterprise will often span multiple organizations.

blocks.text_en: 4.44. Enterprise Architecture Service
blocks.html: 4.44. Enterprise Architecture Service

blocks.text_en:
An encapsulated element of Enterprise Architecture capability that
delivers specific Enterprise Architecture functionality.
blocks.html: An encapsulated element of Enterprise Architecture capability that delivers specific Enterprise Architecture functionality.

blocks.text_en: 4.45. Enterprise Continuum
blocks.html: 4.45. Enterprise Continuum

blocks.text_en:
A categorization mechanism for classifying architecture and Solution
Building Blocks (SBBs) as they evolve from generic to specific
applicability (or vice versa ).
blocks.html: A categorization mechanism for classifying architecture and Solution Building Blocks (SBBs) as they evolve from generic to specific applicability (or vice versa).

blocks.text_en: See also Section 4.10, “Architecture Continuum” and Section 4.75, “Solutions Continuum” .
blocks.html: See also Section 4.10, “Architecture Continuum” and Section 4.75, “Solutions Continuum”.

blocks.text_en: 4.46. Foundation Architecture
blocks.html: 4.46. Foundation Architecture

blocks.text_en:
Generic building blocks, their inter-relationships with other building
blocks, combined with the principles and guidelines that provide a
foundation on which more specific architectures can be built.
blocks.html: Generic building blocks, their inter-relationships with other building blocks, combined with the principles and guidelines that provide a foundation on which more specific architectures can be built.

blocks.text_en: 4.47. Framework
blocks.html: 4.47. Framework

blocks.text_en: A structure for content or process that can be used as a tool to structure thinking, ensuring consistency and completeness.
blocks.html: A structure for content or process that can be used as a tool to structure thinking, ensuring consistency and completeness.

blocks.text_en:
A statement of difference between two states. Used in the context of gap
analysis, where the difference between the Baseline and Target
Architecture is identified.
blocks.html: A statement of difference between two states. Used in the context of gap analysis, where the difference between the Baseline and Target Architecture is identified.

blocks.text_en: Note: Gap analysis is described in the TOGAF Standard — ADM Techniques .
blocks.html:
Note:

Gap analysis is described in the TOGAF Standard — ADM Techniques.

blocks.text_en: 4.49. Governance
blocks.html: 4.49. Governance

blocks.text_en:
The discipline of monitoring and guiding the management of a business
(or IS/IT landscape) to deliver the business outcomes required.
blocks.html: The discipline of monitoring and guiding the management of a business (or IS/IT landscape) to deliver the business outcomes required.

blocks.text_en:
See also Section 4.14, “Architecture Governance” , Section 4.30, “Business Governance” , Section B.27, “Operational Governance” ,
and Appendix B, Glossary of Supplementary Definitions .
blocks.html: See also Section 4.14, “Architecture Governance”, Section 4.30, “Business Governance”, Section B.27, “Operational Governance”, and Appendix B, Glossary of Supplementary Definitions.

blocks.text_en: 4.50. Information
blocks.html: 4.50. Information

blocks.text_en:
Any communication or representation of facts, data, or opinions, in any
medium or form, including textual, numerical, graphic, cartographic, narrative, or audio-visual forms.
blocks.html: Any communication or representation of facts, data, or opinions, in any medium or form, including textual, numerical, graphic, cartographic, narrative, or audio-visual forms.

blocks.text_en: 4.51. Information Technology (IT)
blocks.html: 4.51. Information Technology (IT)

blocks.text_en:
The lifecycle management of information and related technology used by
an organization.
blocks.html: The lifecycle management of information and related technology used by an organization.

blocks.text_en: 4.52. Interoperability
blocks.html: 4.52. Interoperability

blocks.text_en:
The ability to share information and services The ability of two or more systems or components to exchange and use
information The ability of systems to provide and receive services from other
systems and to use the services so interchanged to enable them to
operate effectively together
blocks.html:
1. The ability to share information and services

  2. The ability of two or more systems or components to exchange and use information

  3. The ability of systems to provide and receive services from other systems and to use the services so interchanged to enable them to operate effectively together

blocks.text_en: 4.53. Logical
blocks.html: 4.53. Logical

blocks.text_en: Implementation-independent.
blocks.html: Implementation-independent.

blocks.text_en:
Note: A logical architecture is an implementation-independent definition of
the architecture.
blocks.html:
Note:

A logical architecture is an implementation-independent definition of the architecture.

blocks.text_en: 4.54. Metadata
blocks.html: 4.54. Metadata

blocks.text_en: Data about data, of any sort in any media, that describes the characteristics of an entity.
blocks.html: Data about data, of any sort in any media, that describes the characteristics of an entity.

blocks.text_en: 4.55. Metamodel
blocks.html: 4.55. Metamodel

blocks.text_en:
A model that describes the entities used in building an Architecture
Description, their characteristics, and the key relationships between
those entities.
blocks.html: A model that describes the entities used in building an Architecture Description, their characteristics, and the key relationships between those entities.

blocks.text_en: 4.56. Method
A defined, repeatable approach to address a particular type of problem.
blocks.html: A defined, repeatable approach to address a particular type of problem.

blocks.text_en: 4.57. Modeling
blocks.html: 4.57. Modeling

blocks.text_en:
A technique through construction of models which enables a subject to be
represented in a form that enables reasoning, insight, and clarity
concerning the essence of the subject matter.
blocks.html: A technique through construction of models which enables a subject to be represented in a form that enables reasoning, insight, and clarity concerning the essence of the subject matter.

blocks.text_en: 4.58. Model Kind
blocks.html: 4.58. Model Kind

blocks.text_en: Conventions for a type of modeling.
blocks.html: Conventions for a type of modeling.

blocks.text_en:
Note: An architecture viewpoint references one or more model kinds; an
architecture view incorporates one or more models.
blocks.html:
Note:

An architecture viewpoint references one or more model kinds; an architecture view incorporates one or more models.

blocks.text_en: 4.59. Objective
blocks.html: 4.59. Objective

blocks.text_en:
An organizational aim that is declared in a Specific, Measurable,
Actionable, Realistic, and Timebound (SMART) way. For example, “Increase
capacity utilization by 30% by the end of the year, to support the
planned increase in market share”.
blocks.html: An organizational aim that is declared in a Specific, Measurable, Actionable, Realistic, and Timebound (SMART) way. For example, “Increase capacity utilization by 30% by the end of the year, to support the planned increase in market share”.

blocks.text_en: 4.60. Pattern
blocks.html: 4.60. Pattern

blocks.text_en:
A technique for putting building blocks into context; for example, to
describe a re-usable solution to a problem.
blocks.html: A technique for putting building blocks into context; for example, to describe a re-usable solution to a problem.

blocks.text_en:
Note: Building blocks are what you use: (architecture) patterns can tell you
how you use them, when, why, and what trade-offs you have to make in
doing so.
blocks.html:
Note:

Building blocks are what you use: (architecture) patterns can tell you how you use them, when, why, and what trade-offs you have to make in doing so.

blocks.text_en: See also Section 4.26, “Building Block” .
blocks.html: See also Section 4.26, “Building Block”.

blocks.text_en: 4.61. Physical
blocks.html: 4.61. Physical

blocks.text_en: Real-world, tangible.
blocks.html: Real-world, tangible.

blocks.text_en: Note: A logical architecture is realized through a physical architecture.
blocks.html:
Note:

A logical architecture is realized through a physical architecture.

blocks.text_en: 4.62. Principle
blocks.html: 4.62. Principle

blocks.text_en: See Section 4.19, “Architecture Principle” .
blocks.html: See Section 4.19, “Architecture Principle”.

blocks.text_en: 4.63. Product
blocks.html: 4.63. Product

blocks.text_en: An outcome generated by the business to be offered to customers. Products include materials and/or services.
blocks.html: An outcome generated by the business to be offered to customers. Products include materials and/or services.

blocks.text_en: 4.64. Reference Model (RM)
blocks.html: 4.64. Reference Model (RM)

blocks.text_en:
An abstract framework for understanding significant relationships among
the entities of [an] environment, and for the development of consistent
standards or specifications supporting that environment.
blocks.html: An abstract framework for understanding significant relationships among the entities of [an] environment, and for the development of consistent standards or specifications supporting that environment.

blocks.text_en:
Note: A reference model is based on a small number of unifying concepts and
may be used as a basis for education and explaining standards to a
non-specialist. A reference model is not directly tied to any
standards, technologies, or other concrete implementation details, but
it does seek to provide common semantics that can be used
unambiguously across and between different implementations. Source: OASIS ® ; refer to www.oasis-open.org/committees/soa-rm/faq.php .
blocks.html:
Note:

A reference model is based on a small number of unifying concepts and may be used as a basis for education and explaining standards to a non-specialist. A reference model is not directly tied to any standards, technologies, or other concrete implementation details, but it does seek to provide common semantics that can be used unambiguously across and between different implementations.
Source: OASIS®; refer to www.oasis-open.org/committees/soa-rm/faq.php.

blocks.text_en: 4.65. Requirement
blocks.html: 4.65. Requirement

blocks.text_en:
A statement of need, which is unambiguous, testable or measurable, and
necessary for acceptability.
blocks.html: A statement of need, which is unambiguous, testable or measurable, and necessary for acceptability.

blocks.text_en: 4.66. Roadmap
blocks.html: 4.66. Roadmap

blocks.text_en:
An abstracted plan for business or technology change, typically
operating across multiple disciplines over multiple years. Normally used
in the phrases Technology Roadmap, Architecture Roadmap, etc.
blocks.html: An abstracted plan for business or technology change, typically operating across multiple disciplines over multiple years. Normally used in the phrases Technology Roadmap, Architecture Roadmap, etc.

blocks.text_en: 4.67. Role

The usual or expected behavior of an actor, or the part somebody or something plays in a particular process or event. An actor may have a number of roles The part an individual plays in an organization and the contribution they make through the application of their skills, knowledge,
experience, and abilities
blocks.html:
1. The usual or expected behavior of an actor, or the part somebody or something plays in a particular process or event. An actor may have a number of roles

  2. The part an individual plays in an organization and the contribution they make through the application of their skills, knowledge, experience, and abilities

blocks.text_en: See also Section 4.2, “Actor” .
blocks.html: See also Section 4.2, “Actor”.

blocks.text_en: 4.68. Segment Architecture
blocks.html: 4.68. Segment Architecture

blocks.text_en: A detailed, formal description of areas within an enterprise, used at the program or portfolio level to organize and align change activity.
blocks.html: A detailed, formal description of areas within an enterprise, used at the program or portfolio level to organize and align change activity.

blocks.text_en: See also Section 4.78, “Strategic Architecture” .
blocks.html: See also Section 4.78, “Strategic Architecture”.

blocks.text_en: 4.69. Service
blocks.html: 4.69. Service

blocks.text_en:
An encapsulated element of behavior that provides specific functionality
in response to requests from actors or other services.
blocks.html: An encapsulated element of behavior that provides specific functionality in response to requests from actors or other services.

blocks.text_en: Note: A service has an interface and description.
blocks.html:
Note:

A service has an interface and description.

blocks.text_en: 4.70. Service Orientation
blocks.html: 4.70. Service Orientation

blocks.text_en:
Viewing an enterprise, system, or building block in terms of services
provided and consumed.
blocks.html: Viewing an enterprise, system, or building block in terms of services provided and consumed.

blocks.text_en: See also Section 4.71, “Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA)” .
blocks.html: See also Section 4.71, “Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA)”.

blocks.text_en: 4.71. Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA)
blocks.html: 4.71. Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA)

blocks.text_en: An architectural style that supports service orientation.
blocks.html: An architectural style that supports service orientation.

blocks.text_en: See also Section 4.7, “Architectural Style” and Section 4.70, “Service Orientation” .
blocks.html: See also Section 4.7, “Architectural Style” and Section 4.70, “Service Orientation”.

blocks.text_en: 4.72. Service Portfolio
blocks.html: 4.72. Service Portfolio

blocks.text_en: A collection of services, potentially an interface definition.
blocks.html: A collection of services, potentially an interface definition.

blocks.text_en: Note: It is used in the TOGAF framework to define the requirement for a building block or system.
blocks.html:
Note:

It is used in the TOGAF framework to define the requirement for a building block or system.

blocks.text_en: 4.73. Solution Architecture
blocks.html: 4.73. Solution Architecture

blocks.text_en: A description of a discrete and focused business operation or activity and how IS/IT supports that operation.
blocks.html: A description of a discrete and focused business operation or activity and how IS/IT supports that operation.

blocks.text_en: 4.74. Solution Building Block (SBB)
blocks.html: 4.74. Solution Building Block (SBB)

blocks.text_en: A physical or implementation-specific component that realizes part or all of one or more logical Architecture Building Blocks (ABBs).
blocks.html: A physical or implementation-specific component that realizes part or all of one or more logical Architecture Building Blocks (ABBs).

blocks.text_en: Note: There are business, application, and technology SBBs.
blocks.html:
Note:

There are business, application, and technology SBBs.

blocks.text_en: 4.75. Solutions Continuum
blocks.html: 4.75. Solutions Continuum

blocks.text_en: A categorization mechanism, with increasing detail and specialization, for the components and artifacts stored in the Solutions Landscape or Reference Library (part of the Architecture Repository).
blocks.html: A categorization mechanism, with increasing detail and specialization, for the components and artifacts stored in the Solutions Landscape or Reference Library (part of the Architecture Repository).

blocks.text_en: See also Section 4.45, “Enterprise Continuum” and Section 4.10, “Architecture Continuum” .
blocks.html: See also Section 4.45, “Enterprise Continuum” and Section 4.10, “Architecture Continuum”.

blocks.text_en: 4.76. Stakeholder
blocks.html: 4.76. Stakeholder

blocks.text_en:
An individual, team, organization, or class thereof, having an interest
in a system.
blocks.html: An individual, team, organization, or class thereof, having an interest in a system.

blocks.text_en: 4.77. Standards Library
blocks.html: 4.77. Standards Library

blocks.text_en:
A library of standards that can be used to define the particular
services and other components of an Organization-Specific Architecture.
blocks.html: A library of standards that can be used to define the particular services and other components of an Organization-Specific Architecture.

blocks.text_en: Note: The Standards Library is described in the TOGAF Standard — Architecture Content .
blocks.html:
Note:

The Standards Library is described in the TOGAF Standard — Architecture Content.

blocks.text_en: 4.78. Strategic Architecture
blocks.html: 4.78. Strategic Architecture

blocks.text_en: A summary formal description of the enterprise, providing an organizing framework for operational and change activity, and an executive-level, long-term view for direction setting.
blocks.html: A summary formal description of the enterprise, providing an organizing framework for operational and change activity, and an executive-level, long-term view for direction setting.

blocks.text_en: 4.79. Target Architecture
blocks.html: 4.79. Target Architecture

blocks.text_en:
The description of a future state of the architecture being developed
for an organization.
blocks.html: The description of a future state of the architecture being developed for an organization.

blocks.text_en: Note: There may be several future states developed as a roadmap to show the evolution of the architecture to a target state.
blocks.html:
Note:

There may be several future states developed as a roadmap to show the evolution of the architecture to a target state.

blocks.text_en: 4.80. Taxonomy of Architecture Views
blocks.html: 4.80. Taxonomy of Architecture Views

blocks.text_en:
The organized collection of all architecture views pertinent to an
architecture.
blocks.html: The organized collection of all architecture views pertinent to an architecture.

blocks.text_en: 4.81. Technology Architecture
blocks.html: 4.81. Technology Architecture

blocks.text_en:
A description of the structure and interaction of the technology
services and technology components.
blocks.html: A description of the structure and interaction of the technology services and technology components.

blocks.text_en: Note: Technology Architecture is described in the TOGAF Standard — Architecture Development Method .
blocks.html:
Note:

Technology Architecture is described in the TOGAF Standard — Architecture Development Method.

blocks.text_en: 4.82. Technology Component
blocks.html: 4.82. Technology Component

blocks.text_en:
A technology building block. A generic infrastructure technology that
supports and enables application or data components (directly or indirectly) by providing technology services An encapsulation of technology infrastructure that represents a class of technology product or specific technology product
blocks.html:
1. A technology building block. A generic infrastructure technology that supports and enables application or data components (directly or indirectly) by providing technology services

  2. An encapsulation of technology infrastructure that represents a class of technology product or specific technology product

blocks.text_en: 4.83. Technology Service
blocks.html: 4.83. Technology Service

blocks.text_en: A technical capability required to provide enabling infrastructure that supports the delivery of applications.
blocks.html: A technical capability required to provide enabling infrastructure that supports the delivery of applications.

blocks.text_en: 4.84. Transition Architecture
blocks.html: 4.84. Transition Architecture

blocks.text_en:
A formal description of one state of the architecture at an
architecturally significant point in time.
blocks.html: A formal description of one state of the architecture at an architecturally significant point in time.

blocks.text_en: Note: One or more Transition Architectures may be used to describe the progression in time from the Baseline to the Target Architecture. Transition Architecture is described in the TOGAF Standard — Architecture Content .
blocks.html:
Note:

One or more Transition Architectures may be used to describe the progression in time from the Baseline to the Target Architecture.
Transition Architecture is described in the TOGAF Standard — Architecture Content.

blocks.text_en: 4.85. Value Stream
blocks.html: 4.85. Value Stream

blocks.text_en:
A representation of an end-to-end collection of activities that create
an overall result for a customer, stakeholder, or end user.
blocks.html: A representation of an end-to-end collection of activities that create an overall result for a customer, stakeholder, or end user.

blocks.text_en: 4.86. View
See Section 4.20, “Architecture View” .
blocks.html: See Section 4.20, “Architecture View”.

blocks.text_en: 4.87. Viewpoint
blocks.html: 4.87. Viewpoint

blocks.text_en: See Section 4.21, “Architecture Viewpoint” .
blocks.html: See Section 4.21, “Architecture Viewpoint”.

blocks.text_en: 4.88. Viewpoint Library
blocks.html: 4.88. Viewpoint Library

blocks.text_en:
A collection of the specifications of architecture viewpoints contained
in the Reference Library portion of the Architecture Repository.
blocks.html: A collection of the specifications of architecture viewpoints contained in the Reference Library portion of the Architecture Repository.

blocks.text_en: 4.89. Work Package
blocks.html: 4.89. Work Package

blocks.text_en:
A set of actions identified to achieve one or more objectives for the
business. A work package can be a part of a project, a complete project,
or a program.
blocks.html: A set of actions identified to achieve one or more objectives for the business. A work package can be a part of a project, a complete project, or a program.

blocks.html: A: Referenced Documents

blocks.text_en: B: Glossary of Supplementary Definitions
blocks.html: B: Glossary of Supplementary Definitions

blocks.text_en:
This appendix contains additional definitions to supplement the
definitions contained in Chapter 4, Definitions .
blocks.html: This appendix contains additional definitions to supplement the definitions contained in Chapter 4, Definitions.

blocks.text_en: B.1. Application Software
blocks.html: B.1. Application Software

blocks.text_en: Software entities which have a specific business purpose.
blocks.html: Software entities which have a specific business purpose.

blocks.text_en: B.2. Availability
blocks.html: B.2. Availability

blocks.text_en:
In the context of IT systems, the probability that system functional
capabilities are ready for use by a user at any time, where all time is
considered, including operations, repair, administration, and logistic
time. Availability is further defined by system category for both
routine and priority operations.
blocks.html: In the context of IT systems, the probability that system functional capabilities are ready for use by a user at any time, where all time is considered, including operations, repair, administration, and logistic time. Availability is further defined by system category for both routine and priority operations.

blocks.text_en: B.3. Business System
blocks.html: B.3. Business System

blocks.text_en:
Hardware, software, policy statements, processes, activities, standards,
and people which together implement a business capability.
blocks.html: Hardware, software, policy statements, processes, activities, standards, and people which together implement a business capability.

blocks.text_en: B.4. Catalog
blocks.html: B.4. Catalog

blocks.text_en:
A structured list of architectural outputs of a similar kind, used for
reference. For example, a technology standards catalog or an application
portfolio.
blocks.html: A structured list of architectural outputs of a similar kind, used for reference. For example, a technology standards catalog or an application portfolio.

blocks.text_en: B.5. Client
blocks.html: B.5. Client

blocks.text_en: An application component which requests services from a server.
blocks.html: An application component which requests services from a server.

blocks.text_en: B.6. COBIT
blocks.html: B.6. COBIT

blocks.text_en:
An acronym for Control OBjectives for Information and related
Technology, created by the Information Systems Audit and Control
Association (ISACA) and the IT Governance Institute (ITGI), which
provides a set of recommended best practices for the
governance/management of information systems and technology.
blocks.html: An acronym for Control OBjectives for Information and related Technology, created by the Information Systems Audit and Control Association (ISACA) and the IT Governance Institute (ITGI), which provides a set of recommended best practices for the governance/management of information systems and technology.

blocks.text_en: B.7. Configuration Management
blocks.html: B.7. Configuration Management

blocks.text_en:
A discipline applying technical and administrative direction and
surveillance to:
blocks.html: A discipline applying technical and administrative direction and surveillance to:

blocks.text_en:
Identify and document the functional and physical characteristics of a
configuration item Control changes to those characteristics Record and report changes to processing and implementation status
blocks.html:
• Identify and document the functional and physical characteristics of a configuration item

  • Control changes to those characteristics

  • Record and report changes to processing and implementation status

blocks.text_en:
Also, the management of the configuration of Enterprise Architecture
practice (intellectual property) assets and baselines and the control of
change over of those assets.
blocks.html: Also, the management of the configuration of Enterprise Architecture practice (intellectual property) assets and baselines and the control of change over of those assets.

blocks.text_en: B.8. CxO

The chief officer within a particular function of the business; e.g.,
Chief Executive Officer, Chief Financial Officer, Chief Information
Officer, Chief Technology Officer.
blocks.html: The chief officer within a particular function of the business; e.g., Chief Executive Officer, Chief Financial Officer, Chief Information Officer, Chief Technology Officer.

blocks.text_en: B.9. Data Dictionary
blocks.html: B.9. Data Dictionary

blocks.text_en:
A specialized type of database containing metadata; a repository of
information describing the characteristics of data used to design,
monitor, document, protect, and control data in information systems and
databases; an application system supporting the definition and
management of database metadata.
blocks.html: A specialized type of database containing metadata; a repository of information describing the characteristics of data used to design, monitor, document, protect, and control data in information systems and databases; an application system supporting the definition and management of database metadata.

blocks.text_en: B.10. Data Element
blocks.html: B.10. Data Element

blocks.text_en:
A basic unit of information having a meaning and that may have
subcategories (data items) of distinct units and values.
blocks.html: A basic unit of information having a meaning and that may have subcategories (data items) of distinct units and values.

blocks.text_en: B.11. Database
blocks.html: B.11. Database

blocks.text_en:
A structured or organized collection of data entities, which is to be
accessed by a computer.
blocks.html: A structured or organized collection of data entities, which is to be accessed by a computer.

blocks.text_en: B.12. Database Management System
blocks.html: B.12. Database Management System

blocks.text_en:
A computer application program that accesses or manipulates the
database.
blocks.html: A computer application program that accesses or manipulates the database.

blocks.text_en: B.13. End User
blocks.html: B.13. End User

blocks.text_en: Person who ultimately uses the computer application or output.
blocks.html: Person who ultimately uses the computer application or output.

blocks.text_en: B.14. Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) System
blocks.html: B.14. Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) System

blocks.text_en:
A complete suite of integrated applications that support the major
business support functions of an organization; e.g., Financial
(AP/AR/GL), HR, Payroll, Stock, Order Processing and Invoicing,
Purchasing, Logistics, Manufacturing, etc.
blocks.html: A complete suite of integrated applications that support the major business support functions of an organization; e.g., Financial (AP/AR/GL), HR, Payroll, Stock, Order Processing and Invoicing, Purchasing, Logistics, Manufacturing, etc.

blocks.text_en: B.15. Hardware
blocks.html: B.15. Hardware

blocks.text_en:
The physical infrastructure needed to run software; e.g., servers,
workstations, network equipment, etc.
blocks.html: The physical infrastructure needed to run software; e.g., servers, workstations, network equipment, etc.

blocks.text_en: B.16. Information Domain
blocks.html: B.16. Information Domain

blocks.text_en:
Grouping of information (or data entities) by a set of criteria such as
security classification, ownership, location, etc. In the context of
security, information domains are defined as a set of users, their
information objects, and a security policy.
blocks.html: Grouping of information (or data entities) by a set of criteria such as security classification, ownership, location, etc. In the context of security, information domains are defined as a set of users, their information objects, and a security policy.

blocks.text_en: B.17. Information System (IS)
blocks.html: B.17. Information System (IS)

blocks.text_en: The computer (or IT)-based portion of a business system.
blocks.html: The computer (or IT)-based portion of a business system.

blocks.text_en: B.18. Interaction
blocks.html: B.18. Interaction

blocks.text_en:
A relationship between architectural building blocks (i.e., services or
components) that embodies communication or usage.
blocks.html: A relationship between architectural building blocks (i.e., services or components) that embodies communication or usage.

blocks.text_en: B.19. Interaction Model
blocks.html: B.19. Interaction Model

blocks.text_en:
An architectural view, catalog, or matrix that shows a particular type
of interaction. For example, a diagram showing application integration.
blocks.html: An architectural view, catalog, or matrix that shows a particular type of interaction. For example, a diagram showing application integration.

blocks.text_en: B.20. Interface
blocks.html: B.20. Interface

blocks.text_en:
Interconnection and inter-relationships between, for example, people,
systems, devices, applications, or the user and an application or
device.
blocks.html: Interconnection and inter-relationships between, for example, people, systems, devices, applications, or the user and an application or device.

blocks.text_en: B.21. Key Performance Indicator (KPI)
blocks.html: B.21. Key Performance Indicator (KPI)

blocks.text_en: A way of quantifying the performance of the business or project.
blocks.html: A way of quantifying the performance of the business or project.

blocks.text_en: B.22. Lifecycle
blocks.html: B.22. Lifecycle

blocks.text_en:
The period of time that begins when a system is conceived and ends when
the system is no longer available for use.
blocks.html: The period of time that begins when a system is conceived and ends when the system is no longer available for use.

blocks.text_en: B.23. Managing Successful Programs (MSP)
blocks.html: B.23. Managing Successful Programs (MSP)

blocks.text_en:
A best practice methodology for program management, developed by the UK
Office of Government Commerce (OGC).
blocks.html: A best practice methodology for program management, developed by the UK Office of Government Commerce (OGC).

blocks.text_en: B.24. Matrix
blocks.html: B.24. Matrix

blocks.text_en:
A format for showing the relationship between two (or more)
architectural elements in a grid format.
blocks.html: A format for showing the relationship between two (or more) architectural elements in a grid format.

blocks.text_en: B.25. Metaview
blocks.html: B.25. Metaview

blocks.text_en:
A pattern or template of the view, from which to develop individual
views. Establishes the purposes and audience for a view, the ways in
which the view is documented (e.g., for visual modeling), and the ways
in which it is used (e.g., for analysis).
blocks.html: A pattern or template of the view, from which to develop individual views. Establishes the purposes and audience for a view, the ways in which the view is documented (e.g., for visual modeling), and the ways in which it is used (e.g., for analysis).

blocks.text_en: See also Section 4.21, “Architecture Viewpoint” in Chapter 4, Definitions .
blocks.html: See also Section 4.21, “Architecture Viewpoint” in Chapter 4, Definitions.

blocks.text_en: B.26. Open System
blocks.html: B.26. Open System

blocks.text_en:
A system that implements sufficient open specifications for interfaces,
services, and supporting formats to enable properly engineered
application software:
blocks.html: A system that implements sufficient open specifications for interfaces, services, and supporting formats to enable properly engineered application software:

blocks.text_en: To be ported with minimal changes across a wide range of systems To interoperate with other applications on local and remote systems To interact with users in a style that facilitates user portability
blocks.html:
• To be ported with minimal changes across a wide range of systems

  • To interoperate with other applications on local and remote systems

  • To interact with users in a style that facilitates user portability

blocks.text_en: B.27. Operational Governance
blocks.html: B.27. Operational Governance

blocks.text_en:
The operational performance of systems against contracted performance
levels, the definition of operational performance levels, and the
implementation of systems that ensure effective operation of systems.
blocks.html: The operational performance of systems against contracted performance levels, the definition of operational performance levels, and the implementation of systems that ensure effective operation of systems.

blocks.text_en: See also Section 4.49, “Governance” in Chapter 4, Definitions .
blocks.html: See also Section 4.49, “Governance” in Chapter 4, Definitions.

blocks.text_en: B.28. Packaged Services
blocks.html: B.28. Packaged Services

blocks.text_en:
Services that are acquired from the market from a Commercial
Off-The-Shelf (COTS) vendor, rather than being constructed via code
build.
blocks.html: Services that are acquired from the market from a Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) vendor, rather than being constructed via code build.

blocks.text_en: B.29. Portability
blocks.html: B.29. Portability

blocks.text_en:
The ease with which a system, component, data, or user can be
transferred from one hardware or software environment to another A quality metric that can be used to measure the relative effort to
transport the software for use in another environment or to convert
software for use in another operating environment, hardware
configuration, or software system environment
blocks.html:
1. The ease with which a system, component, data, or user can be transferred from one hardware or software environment to another

  2. A quality metric that can be used to measure the relative effort to transport the software for use in another environment or to convert software for use in another operating environment, hardware configuration, or software system environment

blocks.text_en: B.30. Portfolio
blocks.html: B.30. Portfolio

blocks.text_en:
A collection of programs, projects, and/or operations managed as a group to achieve strategic objectives. For example, project portfolio,
application portfolio, technology portfolio, or service portfolio.
blocks.html: A collection of programs, projects, and/or operations managed as a group to achieve strategic objectives. For example, project portfolio, application portfolio, technology portfolio, or service portfolio.

blocks.text_en: Note: Portfolio management is the act of managing portfolios.
blocks.html:
Note:

Portfolio management is the act of managing portfolios.

blocks.text_en: B.31. PRINCE2
blocks.html: B.31. PRINCE2

The Open Group is a global consortium that enables the achievement of business objectives through technology standards and open source initiatives by fostering a culture of collaboration, inclusivity, and mutual respect among our diverse group of 900+ memberships. Working with suppliers, consortia, and standards bodies to develop consensus and facilitate interoperability, to evolve and integrate specifications and open source technologies
Offering a comprehensive set of services to enhance the operational efficiency of consortia
Developing and operating the industry’s premier certification service and encouraging procurement of certified products
